parts: Here's the story everyone knows: an apple fell on Isaac Newton's head, and he discovered gravity.
That exact moment never happened — at least, not like that.
But a real piece of that same tree has flown into space. Twice.
Today: what Newton actually said happened, and how a tree ended up in orbit.
We'll mark every claim: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you'll know what Newton himself actually claimed — no blow to the head.
And you'll see where pieces of his real tree are flying right now, more than three hundred years later.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Here's where the story comes from: William Stukeley, Newton's friend and first biographer.
Stukeley wrote that Newton told him this himself, years later, in a garden conversation in Kensington.
Newton said the idea of gravity came to him "occasioned by the fall of an apple," while he sat thinking.
John Conduitt, a relative of Newton's, left a similar account.
Documented: Newton himself is the source of the apple story.
Here's what neither account says: that the apple hit him.
No blow to the head, in either telling.
That detail was added later, by popular retelling, not by Newton or his biographers.
Myth.
Stukeley and Conduitt both say they heard it from Newton, late in his life.
Historians think the two accounts may actually trace back to the same source: an elderly Newton, telling the same story to his circle.
So this isn't two independent witnesses — it's probably one story, told twice.
So what did Newton actually claim he was thinking?
Not "ouch." He watched an apple fall straight down, every time, toward the center of the Earth.
Then he asked: what if that same pull reaches all the way to the Moon?
If the Moon is "falling" too — instead of flying off in a straight line — that constant fall is what keeps it in orbit.
Here's the twist most people miss: that tree is not a legend. It's real, and it's still alive.
It stands today at Woolsthorpe Manor, the farmhouse where Newton grew up.
A storm, in the early eighteen hundreds, knocked the original trunk down — but it regrew from its own roots.
Tree-ring dating puts it at over four hundred years old. Documented.
And here's where it gets strange: a piece of that exact tree has flown to space.
In twenty ten, a fragment of its wood flew aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, carried by British astronaut Piers Sellers.
It spent twelve days in orbit.
It returned to the Royal Society on July sixth, twenty ten. Documented, straight from the Royal Society's own announcement.
A few years later, the same tree went to space again — this time as seeds.
Between twenty fourteen and twenty sixteen, seeds from this tree flew to the International Space Station with British astronaut Tim Peake.
Back on Earth, they were germinated at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, and grown into saplings.
Tim Peake himself later planted one of those saplings back at Woolsthorpe Manor.
A few details here are still soft.
How long those seeds actually spent in microgravity is reported as "around six months" — but that figure comes from news coverage, not a lab record we've confirmed directly.
And the exact year of the storm that first felled the tree is given differently by different sources — so we'll call it "the early eighteen hundreds," not one fixed date.
Let's count what we actually know.
Newton himself told this story, apple and all: documented.
The apple hitting his head: myth.
The storm's exact year, and the seeds' exact time in orbit: still disputed, or simply unconfirmed.
So no, an apple never hit Isaac Newton on the head.
He watched one fall straight down, and wondered if the Moon was falling too.
And three hundred years later, pieces of that same tree have already answered a question he never got to ask: what does gravity look like, up there?
